author: Johanna Spyri

pages.text:
The little old town of Maienfeld lies at the foot of a high mountain range, where a wide valley stretches out below, its green meadows bright in the summer sunshine. A narrow footpath winds steeply up from the valley floor toward the heights above, where the air grows cool and the grasses grow short and thick between grey boulders.

One fine June morning, a tall young woman named Dete came climbing this steep path, leading by the hand a small child dressed in so many layers of clothing that the little one looked quite round, like a barrel. The child was perhaps five years old, with bright dark eyes and healthy red cheeks that showed she was sturdy and well.

Dete herself moved quickly up the path despite the heat, for she was anxious to complete her errand. She carried a large bundle under one arm and kept a firm grip on the child with her other hand.

Halfway up the mountain, they met their neighbor Barbel, who was coming down the path with her empty milk pails. Barbel stopped in surprise to see Dete with the child.

"Good morning, Dete," said Barbel. "Is this little one your niece — the orphan child? Where are you taking her, dressed up like that in all this heat?"

"I am taking her to her grandfather, the Alm-Uncle, up on the mountain," said Dete. "She must live with him now. I cannot keep her any longer."

Barbel stopped walking and stared. "You cannot mean it, Dete! You are taking that poor little thing to live with the old Alm-Uncle? He is a strange, fierce old man. Everyone in the valley avoids him. He barely speaks to his neighbors and has not come down to the village in years. What will become of the child up there?"

"He is her grandfather, and it is his duty to take care of her," said Dete firmly. "I have done my duty long enough. The child's father — the Alm-Uncle's own son — died in an accident two years ago, and her mother had been ill with fever for a long time before that and died not long after. I took little Heidi in and cared for her as best I could, but now I have found good work in Frankfurt, and I cannot bring a child of five along with me."

"But what do you know about his character?" Barbel pressed. "They say he left the village under a cloud many years ago — that he spent all his money and did something he was ashamed of. Nobody really knows his full story."

"I know what I know," said Dete, and she walked on. "He is Heidi's grandfather and that is enough."

During all of this conversation the child called Heidi had been trotting along between the two women, listening quietly. Her name was really Adelheid, but the short form Heidi was all anyone had ever called her.

As the morning grew warmer and the path steeper, Heidi began to feel very hot indeed under all her layers. She was wearing two dresses, one over the other, a thick red scarf, and stout shoes. Beads of perspiration stood out on her little forehead.

"Are you tired, Heidi?" asked Dete, glancing down.

"No," said Heidi, "but I am very hot."

Barbel had turned back toward the village, and so Dete and Heidi climbed on alone. The path grew more winding as they rose higher, and the meadows gave way to patches of pine forest where the air smelled sharply of resin. Through the trees Heidi caught glimpses of the great blue sky above and heard the sound of rushing water from a mountain stream somewhere nearby.

Suddenly the path opened out onto a high meadow, and Heidi stopped to stare at the wide, bright world spread before her. Far below, the green valley was small and toy-like. The mountain peaks above gleamed with snow in the clear morning light. She drew a deep breath of the cool, flower-scented air.

"Come along," said Dete, pulling her hand. "We are not there yet."

A little farther up the path, they met a boy of about eleven years old who was driving a small herd of goats before him, whistling and calling to them as they scrambled over the rocks. He was a thin, wiry boy with a weather-browned face and quick, bright eyes. This was Peter, the goat-herd, who came from the village below every morning to collect the goats from the farmers and drive them up to the high mountain pastures for the day.

"Good morning, Peter," said Dete. "Are you going up to the Alm?"

"Yes," said Peter, eyeing Heidi with curiosity.

Before Dete could say another word, Heidi had pulled her hand free. In a moment she had dropped behind a large boulder by the side of the path, and when she reappeared she was carrying her thick red scarf and her extra dress, which she had stripped off as quickly as she could. She set them both on the rock with satisfaction and looked up, much more comfortable.

"I am going to walk with Peter and the goats," she announced.

Dete frowned but was too tired from the steep climb to argue. "Very well, but don't go too fast and don't fall." She picked up Heidi's discarded clothing with a sigh.

Heidi ran ahead with Peter, and the two children and the goats went scrambling up the rocky path together. Heidi laughed with delight as the goats jostled and bleated around her.

Dete climbed on more slowly, thinking about the old man who lived alone on the mountain. The villagers in Maienfeld called him simply the Alm-Uncle, and they were somewhat afraid of him. He had not always lived up here in this lonely fashion. When he was a young man he had been wealthy, with fine lands in the valley, but he had lost everything through reckless living. Then, many years ago, he had suddenly appeared on the mountain above the village, built himself a rough hut, and had lived there ever since, seeing almost nobody.

He had one son, Tobias, who had grown up, become a carpenter, and married a good woman named Adelheid. But Tobias had died in an accident only a few years after the marriage, and Adelheid, already ill, had died soon after of grief and exhaustion, leaving behind a tiny daughter, also called Adelheid — little Heidi.

Dete had taken in the orphan child and done her best. But now her own life called her away, and the old grandfather would simply have to do his duty.

At last the path curved around a rocky shoulder of the mountain and the hut came into view — a solid, weather-beaten wooden building with a wide bench along its front wall, standing on a rocky ledge above a slope of rough meadow. Behind it rose the dark pine forest, and above the forest the great bare mountain crags. The view over the valley below was magnificent.

An old man sat on the bench outside the hut, smoking a long pipe and gazing out across the valley. He was tall and broad-shouldered even in old age, with a thick grey beard and heavy grey eyebrows that jutted out over sharp, piercing eyes. He wore rough mountain clothes and sturdy boots. His face was deeply weathered by years of sun and wind. As Dete and Heidi came up the path toward him, he did not rise or call out a greeting, but simply watched them come, his expression unreadable.

Heidi trotted straight up to him without hesitation. "Good morning, Grandfather," she said, and held out her hand.

The old man looked down at her for a long moment. His sharp eyes travelled slowly over her face, studying it. Then he took her small hand in his large, rough one and shook it.

"So," he said, in a low, gruff voice. "Who are you?"

"I am Heidi," said the child. "I am Tobias's daughter. Aunt Dete says I am to live here now."

The old man turned his sharp gaze on Dete, who had arrived behind Heidi and was catching her breath after the long climb. His expression was not welcoming.

"And what is the meaning of this?" he said to Dete. His voice was calm but his eyes were cold.

Dete stood her ground. "It is as the child says. She is your grandchild and it is your duty to take her in."

"My duty," repeated the old man slowly. He looked at Dete with those sharp, cold eyes. "And if I do not choose to take her?"

"Then I don't know what will become of her," said Dete, more quietly. "I have kept her for two years. I have a good position in Frankfurt that I cannot refuse. She is your son's child, after all. It falls to you."

For a long moment the old man said nothing. He looked down at Heidi again. She had not moved away but stood calmly beside him, returning his gaze with serious dark eyes, neither frightened nor shy.

While the old man and Dete argued in low, stiff voices, Heidi had been looking around her with great interest. She noticed a small wooden enclosure attached to the side of the hut, and in it two goats — one white and one brown — looking back at her over the fence. She went over to them at once and pressed her face against the rough wooden boards.

"What are their names?" she called back to her grandfather.

He broke off his conversation and glanced toward her. "The white one is Little Swan," he said after a pause, "and the brown one is Little Bear."

"Hello, Little Swan. Hello, Little Bear," said Heidi softly, and reached her hand through the boards to touch the white goat's nose. The goat sniffed at her and then stood still, allowing her to stroke it.

Dete saw that arguing further with the old man would take all day and might not succeed in any case. She had already said what needed to be said. The grandfather would simply have to manage. She took a step back toward the path.

"Goodbye, then, Heidi," she called. "I'll come and visit when I can."

"Goodbye, Aunt Dete," said Heidi cheerfully from beside the goat pen, not looking up.

Dete turned and walked quickly back down the path before the grandfather could protest further. She did not look back. Behind her she heard the old man say something short and sharp, but she was already out of earshot.

The grandfather looked at his granddaughter for a moment. She had turned back to the goats and was murmuring to them softly in a comfortable way, as though she had known them all her life.

He breathed in slowly. The child had not cried. She had not clung to her aunt or begged not to be left. She had simply accepted the situation and turned her attention to what was interesting. He did not know what to make of that.

"Come inside and see where you will sleep," he said at last.

Heidi followed him without hesitation into the dark hut. Inside there was one large room with a fireplace, a table, a bench, and the old man's sleeping loft above. She looked at everything with bright, curious eyes.

"Where will I sleep?" she asked.

"We shall find a place," said the grandfather, and something in his voice was just a little less cold than before.
